title: Devanagari
hook: one bar, one word, except when four words share it
tomorrow: Sam wants a Sanskrit tattoo for graduation. good idea?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devanagari's danda: one stroke for half a verse, two for the whole, the written memory of a voice's pause. Today, a rule that seems to break.

Say did you eat yet, fast, to a friend across a kitchen, and it comes out as one long slur. English speakers do that all day and never write it down. Sanskrit writes it down. So here's the puzzle. A few days ago the rule was one bar, one word. Then the first bar of the Gita's line about action: karmanyevadhikaraste. One unbroken head line. And in translation it's a whole clause.

Take it apart and there are several words inside. Karmani: in action. Eva: only. Adhikarah: the right. Te: yours. Your right is in action only. Said aloud at speaking speed, their edges melt into each other. The i at the end of karmani meets the e of eva and turns into a y: karmany eva. The a at the end of eva meets the a that begins adhikarah, and the two become one long a: evadhikarah. The h at the end of adhikarah turns into an s before te. The grammarians call this sandhi, joining, and Panini sets out rules for exactly these meetings. Sanskrit writes what the mouth does, so printed Sanskrit often runs words together under one head line, and a reader learns to find the seams. Some books for learners split them with spaces or hyphens; the sounds stay joined. So the rule from before still holds, with an asterisk: one bar is one stretch of sound, and in Sanskrit a stretch of sound can carry several words. Read slowly and the seams show up, and the line says what it says: your right is in the action only.
screen: `SEVERAL WORDS UNDER ONE BAR.` · `I BECOMES Y. A AND A BECOME LONG A.` · `SANDHI: SOUNDS JOINING AT THE EDGES.` · `ONE BAR, ONE STRETCH OF SOUND.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes close and notice where one breath ends and the next begins. Don't try to find a gap; just notice whether the out-breath melts into the in-breath, the way two words melt at their edges. Stay with that joint, breath after breath.
Devanagari: a script where one head line can carry several words joined by sandhi, written just as they're said.
Pocket this: Devanagari, where one bar is one stretch of sound, and some stretches hold several words. Rest well.

howItsDone: Sanskrit readers learn to undo sandhi, splitting a printed run of words into its parts; many learners' editions print the split words alongside the joined text.

chat.meaning: Sandhi joins words where their sounds meet, and Sanskrit writes them that way, so one bar can hold several words.

sandhi.meaning: joining: the sound changes where words meet

Panini.meaning: the ancient grammarian whose rules describe Sanskrit's sounds

adhikarah.meaning: the right, in the Gita's line about action

sources.ref: Panini, Ashtadhyayi 6.1.77, 6.1.101 and 8.3.34 (the sandhi rules at work in the line)

notes: Answers 1436's question. Sandhi in 2.47: karmaṇi + eva > karmaṇy eva (i to y before a vowel, Ashtadhyayi 6.1.77); eva + adhikāraḥ > evādhikāraḥ (like vowels to a long vowel, 6.1.101); adhikāraḥ + te > adhikāras te (visarga to s before t, 8.3.34). Confirm the rule numbers.

The hook says 'several words' in the voice; the chat has Priya quoting Nani as 'like four words', which is what the text has (karmaṇi, eva, adhikāraḥ, te). Paraphrase of the clause: 'your right is in action only'.
Gloss 'adhikarah' gives 'uh-dhi-KAH-ruh' (visarga not voiced in the sound-out). 'Panini' gloss says 'ancient' without a date.
